\chapter{Sun and Shade}
\label{ch:sa-sun-and-shade}
\hlchaptermodality{46}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the sun, a ray, light, shade and heat in Sanskrit.}

Complete SA-C46-heat and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[raviḥ]{\sk{रविः} (raviḥ) — the sun}

\label{lesson:SA-C46-sun}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{saṁvatsaraḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{रविः}}
\textbf{\sk{रविः}} (\emph{raviḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the sun\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{रविः}} is the sun: the disc itself, not the light it sends.

You have \sk{आकाशः} for the open sky and \sk{चन्द्रः} for the moon. \textbf{\sk{रविः}} is the third thing overhead, and the one the other two are measured against.

Sanskrit keeps several sun-words and this one has no agreed cousin outside India, so its history stops at the border. Its life since then has not: Hindi still calls Sunday \emph{ravivār}, so the word gets said once a week by people who have never studied it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third thing overhead, beside the sky and the moon.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raviḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{saṁvatsaraḥ}, then \emph{raviḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{रविः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the sun\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raśmiḥ]{\sk{रश्मिः} (raśmiḥ) — a ray}

\label{lesson:SA-C46-ray}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{raviḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{रश्मिः}}
\textbf{\sk{रश्मिः}} (\emph{raśmiḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a ray\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{रश्मिः}} is a ray: one line of light, reaching down from \sk{रविः}.

The same word means a rein or a cord held in the hand, and the two senses share one picture — something long and thin, stretched from a holder to the thing it holds. A ray reaches out of the sun the way a rein reaches out of a fist.

That doubling is worth noticing, because it shows how Sanskrit builds: not two words for two things, but one shape lent to both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The sun, and the line of light it lets down.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raśmiḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{raviḥ}, then \emph{raśmiḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{रश्मिः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a ray\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prakāśaḥ]{\sk{प्रकाशः} (prakāśaḥ) — light}

\label{lesson:SA-C46-light}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{raśmiḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{प्रकाशः}}
\textbf{\sk{प्रकाशः}} (\emph{prakāśaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{प्रकाशः}} is light: brightness itself, and the state of a thing being visible at all.

You met a piece meaning \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to be seen\textquotedblright{} once before, sitting inside \textbf{\sk{आकाशः}}, the open sky. \textbf{\sk{प्रकाशः}} is that very piece with \emph{pra-}, \textquotedblleft{}forward\textquotedblright{}, in front of it — light as shining sent out.

So the sky and the light in it are built out of one word, parting only at the small piece each carries at the front. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{अः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Light, and the piece it shares with the sky.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prakāśaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{raśmiḥ}, then \emph{prakāśaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{प्रकाशः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chāyā]{\sk{छाया} (chāyā) — shade, a shadow}

\label{lesson:SA-C46-shade}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{prakāśaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{छाया}}
\textbf{\sk{छाया}} (\emph{chāyā}) — \textquotedblleft{}shade, a shadow\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{छाया}} is shade, and equally the shadow a thing throws.

You have \sk{छत्रम्} for the parasol. \textbf{\sk{छाया}} is what the parasol makes: the cool patch, not the object holding it up. One is the tool and the other is the result, and now you can name both.

Greek \emph{skiā}, \textquotedblleft{}shadow\textquotedblright{}, is the same word, and English \emph{shine} is usually put in the family too — brightness and the dark it casts named from one root. Feminine, ending in \textbf{-\sk{आ}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The thing the parasol makes, told apart from the parasol.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāyā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{prakāśaḥ}, then \emph{chāyā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{छाया} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}shade, a shadow\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tāpaḥ]{\sk{तापः} (tāpaḥ) — heat}

\label{lesson:SA-C46-heat}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{prakāśaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{chāyā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तापः}}
\textbf{\sk{तापः}} (\emph{tāpaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}heat\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{तापः}} is heat: the warmth of the sun on a back, and by an easy stretch the heat of trouble.

It stands on \emph{tap}, \textquotedblleft{}to be hot, to burn\textquotedblright{} — the same root under \emph{tapas}, the heat a person is said to build up by hard practice. Sanskrit treats effort and warmth as one thing.

Latin \emph{tepēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be warm\textquotedblright{}, is that root gone west, and English took \emph{tepid} straight from it. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{अः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things about light and warmth: the sun, a ray, light, shade, heat.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tāpaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{raviḥ} and \emph{tāpaḥ} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{तापः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}heat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
